report:
## Conclusion

An unqualified **“no” is not supported**. The evidence indicates that widespread mask wearing **can reduce SARS-CoV-2 infections**, but the population-level effect is generally **modest, context-dependent, and not uniformly demonstrated**.

The strongest direct evidence is a cluster-randomized trial in 600 Bangladeshi villages involving 342,183 adults. Community mask distribution and promotion substantially increased mask use and reduced symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections, with surgical masks appearing more effective than cloth masks. Because the intervention changed community behavior, it is especially relevant to population-wide masking rather than merely individual protection: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abi9069

A PNAS evidence review concluded that masks reduce transmission through both source control and wearer protection, and that benefits become greatest when adoption is widespread because infected people may be asymptomatic or presymptomatic: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2014564118

However, the evidence is not definitive. Cochrane’s review of randomized trials found generally low-to-moderate certainty and did not establish a clear effect across all mask interventions and settings: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD006207_do-physical-measures-such-hand-washing-or-wearing-masks-stop-or-slow-down-spread-respiratory-viruses

Cochrane also warned that this review was widely misinterpreted as proving “masks do not work”; it did not specifically answer every question about population-level COVID-19 masking: https://www.cochrane.org/about-us/news/statement-physical-interventions-interrupt-or-reduce-spread-respiratory-viruses-review

**Bottom line:** widespread, consistent use of well-fitting, higher-quality masks likely reduces infections, particularly during high transmission, but masks are a partial measure rather than a guarantee.
